title: Micah: what is good (Micah 6:8)
hookLine: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God"
last: DOEST THOU WELL TO BE ANGRY.

lines: RAMS, RIVERS OF OIL, A FIRSTBORN?
cards: The sixth chapter of Micah opens like a courtroom, and the mountains are the jury. In the King James: "Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD's controversy."
God makes the case: I brought you up out of Egypt, I sent you Moses and Aaron and Miriam. What have I done to you? And the people start bidding.
Burnt offerings? Calves a year old? Thousands of rams?
Ten thousand rivers of oil? Then the worst bid of all: shall I give my firstborn for my sin? Then a voice cuts in, and the answer is small.

teach.b: It begins: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good." Shown already. Not a secret, not a new demand.
Then: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." Three verbs, each pointing a different way. Do justly points outward, at how you treat people.

teach.h: DO JUSTLY: MISHPAT, A FAIR RULING.
teach.b: The Hebrew is mishpat: a fair ruling, what a good judge does at the city gate, done with your hands, at work and in the market. Love mercy points inward, at what you want.
The Hebrew behind mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal kindness that goes past what's owed. And Micah doesn't say do mercy. He says love it.

teach.h: LOVE MERCY: CHESED, WANTED, NOT JUST DONE.
teach.b: Some readers hear the difference this way: justice can be done through gritted teeth, but chesed has to be wanted.

Walk humbly points alongside. Not a leap, not a performance: a walk, at walking pace, with God. English translations render that phrase in more than one way, humbly or modestly, but either way it's quiet.
Now look at the bidding war.

teach.h: NOT A BIGGER GIFT, A DIFFERENT LIFE.
teach.b: The people kept raising the price, rams, rivers, a child, as if the right gift could stand in for a fairer life. Micah's answer isn't a bigger offering.
It's a different kind of thing: a way of living, with people and with God, on an ordinary weekday.
That doesn't throw out the offerings or the Torah; two chapters earlier, Micah pictures the nations climbing to the Temple mountain to learn it. The answer asks that the life match the gift.

how: Micah 6:8 is read in synagogue at the end of a prophetic reading from Micah, and it is quoted in Jewish teaching on justice and kindness.

o: the prophet who told the people to bring a thousand rams
the prophet who answered the bidding war with three verbs
a judge who held court with the mountains as the jury

games.q: what is good — tap the pairs.

s: in the chapter, the people offer bigger and bigger gifts
burnt offerings, calves, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, even a firstborn.
Micah says what is good is a secret for prophets
"he hath shewed thee, O man, what is good." it was shown already.
it says love mercy. the Hebrew word is chesed, loyal kindness.

games.q: you've been called to account before the mountains, and you want to make it right with God. what do you bring?
o: thousands of rams and rivers of oil.
the most precious thing you have.
to do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
games.why: the answer isn't a bigger gift. it's a way of living: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God."

practice: Take the three verbs one at a time.

Do justly: find one place where something is a little unfair and your hand is in it, and name what fair would look like; love mercy: think of someone who owes you an apology or a favor, and notice whether any part of you wants to let it go.
Walk humbly: just walk with the breath, nothing to prove, and if you pray, say the verse slowly, phrase by phrase.

wordCard.voice: Micah. A prophet of the Twelve, who answered a bidding war with three verbs: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: steady, loyal kindness; the word behind "mercy" in Micah 6:8.

carryVoice: Your line: justly, mercy, humbly. Short enough to carry in a pocket. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.
